source.title: Can Pre-training Indicators Reliably Predict Fine-tuning Outcomes of LLMs?
source.authors: Hansi Zeng; Kai Hui; Honglei Zhuang; Zhen Qin; Zhenrui Yue; Hamed Zamani; Dana Alon

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream-task predictability using pairwise prediction from pre-training indicators across same-size model variants, rather than measuring scaling laws across model sizes, tokens or compute.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling-law results from other work but does not test them. Its own relevant outcomes are pairwise prediction accuracies for post-SFT task performance; the model variants are all 1B parameters trained on 100B tokens. Results are reported as aggregate predictions over pairs, not separately for each model.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether held-out perplexity predicts downstream post-SFT performance among 50 same-size (1B, 100B-token) variants. It finds conventional causal-LM perplexity ranks pairs worse than chance. That bears on V6's 'predictable with pretraining loss' clause in a fixed-scale setting and argues the clause needs restating. It does not vary scale, so it tests nothing else in the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that conventional perplexity is a misleading, even negatively correlated, indicator of post-SFT performance among same-size, same-compute variants. Span-corruption perplexity, k-shot proxies and a learning-to-compare classifier cut error by over 50%. Prediction is reliable only for large performance gaps and for shortlisting top candidates. Extending the results to larger scales is left for future work.
record.recipe_differences: Measures predictive accuracy for post-SFT performance among same-size variants; does not fit or test the original scaling-law relationships.
record.method_sensitivity: Predictive accuracy varies by proxy and target SFT task; the paper also reports dependence on the size of the true SFT-performance gap and on which pre-training-objective comparison is made.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed scale, few-shot RAG performance predicts which model is better after SFT in about .70–.77 of pairs. A LightGBM classifier over five proxies reaches about .73–.75 and transfers across SFT tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Among same-size models, few-shot task performance (not pretraining loss) predicts post-SFT ranking moderately well.

record.problems: All tested variants have the same stated size and token count, so the study does not test scaling trends. Its main results aggregate pairwise comparisons among 50 variants; classifier results use 20 random splits. The authors note limited reliability for small performance gaps and leave generalization to larger scales and broader tasks for future work.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant numerical prediction results from Tables 1 or 2 were left out. Figure 4 reports quantile-dependent accuracy mostly as plotted values; the text describes the trend but does not provide individual task-by-quantile numbers, so those were not transcribed as numerical rows. Figure 2's objective-comparison plots are described qualitatively, with only selected comparisons and values stated in prose; no separate rows were added for unreported plotted values.

untested.parts: All of it: no loss measured across parameters, tokens or compute.
All of it: no fits and no extrapolation.
All of it: no allocation under a fixed compute budget.
All of it: architecture is fixed.
All of it: no power-law fits in other modalities or regimes.
Improvement of downstream performance with scale. Every model has the same size and compute, so only the pretraining-loss clause is tested, and only within a fixed scale.
All of it: no exponents or compute-optimal splits are fitted.

missing.what: PPL-CLM pairwise accuracy by quantile of true SFT performance gap. Accuracy decreases as the gap grows, strengthening the reversal.

PPL-CLM and PPL-SC accuracy for pairs differing only in objective, data re-weighting or tagging/length filtering. Needed to see whether the perplexity reversal survives when the objective is held fixed.
missing.locator: Section 3 case study, Figure 2; Appendix C, Figures 6–7

missing.what: Per-model perplexity and SFT scores. For example, models 6–10 (SC, varying learning rate) show inverse PPL-CLM falling while SFT-CMS rises. However, the column alignment in the extracted table appears garbled.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'supports' label rested mostly on k-shot and classifier rows, which measure the study's own proxies, not pretraining loss or scale, so it is removed. The PPL-CLM reversal is probably confounded with pretraining objective: non-CLM objectives have higher CLM perplexity but better SFT scores. Figures 2 and 6–7 and Table 6 would show whether it holds within a single objective. The paper itself contrasts this fixed-scale result with the loss–downstream correlation seen across scale.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure held-out pre-training loss as a function of parameters, tokens or compute.
Does not fit power laws on small runs or test predictions on larger runs.
Does not compare parameter/token allocations under fixed compute or estimate allocation exponents.
Does not vary architecture depth, width or other architecture details.
Tests neither other modalities nor repeated-data, fine-tuning-scaling or transfer power laws.

Tests prediction of post-SFT performance among 1B variants, not performance trends with scale; does not test the general relationship between pre-training loss and downstream performance across model sizes.
Does not fit scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits, nor test how parameter counting, training schedules or scaling-law fitting choices affect them.

relationships.condition: Conventional causal-LM held-out perplexity, 50 same-size 1B variants differing in objective, data mix, learning rate and filtering; post-SFT CMS/RAG/CBQA
relationships.reason: Lower CLM perplexity predicts the worse SFT model in most pairs: accuracy .33–.38, below 0.5 chance (T1-01–T1-03, T2-01–T2-03). Section 5.1 adds that PPL-CLM accuracy falls as the true performance gap widens (text only).
relationships.display_finding: Perplexity selected the better fine-tuned model with only 0.33–0.38 accuracy, below 0.5 chance, and prediction accuracy fell as actual performance gaps widened.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: Conventional causal-LM held-out perplexity, 50 same-size 1B variants differing in objective, data mix, learning rate and filtering; post-SFT CMS/RAG/CBQA
source_check.reason: T1-01–T1-03 report inverse-perplexity ranking accuracies .332, .380 and .354, below .5 chance; T2-01–T2-03 repeat the reversal on test splits. Section 5.1 explicitly reports decreasing accuracy as performance gaps widen.

relationships.condition: Span-corruption held-out perplexity as the loss measure, same fixed-scale setting
relationships.reason: A different perplexity definition predicts downstream ranking above chance but weakly (.61–.70; T1-04–T1-06). Whether loss predicts downstream results at fixed scale depends on which loss is measured.
relationships.display_finding: Downstream ranking prediction was above chance but weak at 0.61–0.70, making predictive quality depend on the perplexity definition.
